title: Capstone: Ship a Small Release
description: Plan and model a focused release using branches, commits, integration, and tags.

blocks.content: A release is when you decide the code is ready for users. The Git part of a release is straightforward: you mark the exact commit that shipped with a **tag**, so you can always find it again. Tags are permanent labels that never move, unlike branches.

## Putting It All Together

Here's the complete flow from idea to release using everything you've learned:

```
# 1. Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull

# 2. Create a feature branch
git switch -c feature/payment-update

# 3. Work and commit
git add .
git commit -m "update payment provider to Stripe v3"

# 4. Push and open a pull request for review
git push origin feature/payment-update

# 5. After approval, merge into main (usually done via the platform UI)
git switch main
git merge feature/payment-update
git push

# 6. Tag the release
git tag v2.1.0
git push origin v2.1.0

# 7. Clean up the feature branch
git branch -d feature/payment-update
git push origin --delete feature/payment-update
```

## Tagging Conventions

Most teams use **semantic versioning**: `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

- `MAJOR` - breaking change (old code might not work)
- `MINOR` - new feature, backwards compatible
- `PATCH` - bug fix

So `v2.1.0` means: major version 2, first new feature added, no patches yet.

## Checking Out a Past Release

Need to look at or deploy an older version?
```
git checkout v1.0.0
```

This puts you in "detached HEAD" state - you can look around, but create a new branch before making changes.

blocks.question: What makes a tag different from a branch?
options: Tags can only be created by team leads
Tags are only visible on GitHub, not locally
Tags are permanent labels that never move; branches move forward with each commit
Tags can contain commit messages; branches cannot
blocks.explanation: A branch moves forward every time you make a new commit on it. A tag is fixed forever at the commit it was created on. This makes tags ideal for marking releases - `v1.0.0` will always point to the exact code that shipped.

blocks.prompt: Tag the current commit as v1.0.0 and push the tag to origin.
acceptedAnswers:
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
